analysis.one_liner: Repeals the decades-old ban on exporting American crude oil.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to four House committees and subcommittees and never came up for a vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since the 1970s energy crisis, most US crude oil generally could not be sold to foreign buyers. This bill would repeal that restriction across several federal laws, require the Commerce Department to issue export licenses to almost any country not under US sanctions, and let the President block exports only during a declared national emergency for up to 90 days at a time. It was introduced in April 2014 and died without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Crude oil producers — especially companies drilling from the shale boom — gain access to world markets where prices were higher than prices for domestic crude. Oil traders and export facilities also gain new business.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the presidential authority under the Energy Policy and Conservation Act to restrict oil exports, the Mineral Leasing Act export limits, and the Outer Continental Shelf export limits [S2].

Requires the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security to grant crude export licenses to any country unless it is under US sanctions or designated off-limits for national security reasons [S2].
Retains only a limited presidential power to ban crude exports during a national emergency, for 90 days at a time, with each ban subject to congressional review [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Domestic refiners, which had been buying US crude at a discount, would face higher feedstock costs. To the extent domestic crude prices rise toward world prices, drivers and businesses could pay more for gasoline and diesel.

drawbacks.text: Lifting the export ban would tie domestic crude prices to higher world prices, which tends to raise what American drivers and businesses pay at the pump; domestic refiners that relied on discounted US crude would also lose their cost advantage.

The bill strips away broad export restrictions that were originally designed to protect US energy supply, leaving only a narrow 90-day presidential ban usable during a declared national emergency [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go mainly to oil producers who could sell crude abroad at higher prices. The costs fall on domestic refiners and, through higher fuel prices, on consumers. Proponents would argue exports encourage more drilling and lower trade deficits, but the bill's most direct financial effect is a transfer to oil producers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee: it was sent to four House committees and three subcommittees, none of which acted, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael McCaul introduced the bill on April 1, 2014, joined by Rep. John Culberson, with eight Republican cosponsors total [S1].
It was referred to the Foreign Affairs, Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, and Rules Committees, and then to subcommittees in early April and June 2014 [S5].
No committee reported the bill and no chamber ever voted on it before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Domestic refiners and consumers of gasoline and diesel are better off that the ban stayed in place during this Congress, since discounted domestic crude remained available to US refineries. The oil producers who backed the bill got nothing from it in the 113th Congress.

for.name: Rep. Michael McCaul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Crude Oil Export Act to repeal the crude oil export ban.

for.name: Rep. John Culberson
for.what_they_did: Joined McCaul in introducing the bill.

against.name: House committee leadership (Foreign Affairs, Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, Rules)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled action; no committee reported it, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters (the sponsor plus eight cosponsors, plus the original cosponsor counted among them) were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and no floor vote ever occurred to reveal a broader split [S4].

industries.note: The bill's death kept the export ban in place, so US producers continued selling into a domestic market priced below world levels. Their gain under the bill would have come directly from higher prices for fuel and petroleum products used by ordinary Americans, so their interest ran against consumers'.
Refiners had been buying discounted US crude because it could not be exported; the ban's survival protected that advantage. The bill would have raised their feedstock costs.
Terminal, pipeline, and export-service businesses saw no new export market open. This is a narrower commercial interest than producers, though its gains would have tracked the producer gain.
